analysis.one_liner: Bans making or selling semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, exempting existing owners.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, with a long list of specific rifles, pistols, and shotguns named in the bill text [S3]. People who already owned these guns could keep them, but would have to store them securely, and any private sale or transfer would require a licensed dealer to run a background check [S2]. It would also let states use existing federal grant money to pay people who turn these guns in through buy-back programs, require serial numbers and manufacture dates on new magazines, order police to be notified when a banned purchaser tries to buy a grandfathered weapon, and direct the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives to build a rating system for how dangerous firearms are and a database tracking mass shootings [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in places where mass shootings with military-style rifles happen — schools, workplaces, churches, concerts — if the restrictions reduce access to weapons capable of firing many rounds quickly. Hunters and sport shooters keep their guns: bolt-action, lever-action, pump, and thousands of specific hunting and competition models are explicitly listed as exempt in an appendix to the bill [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, with exceptions for law enforcement and a list of exempt firearms [S2].

Lets current owners keep grandfathered weapons but requires secure storage and a dealer-run background check before any private sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon; possession of grandfathered large-capacity magazines is allowed but no new sales or transfers of them [S2].
Allows states and local governments to use Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to compensate people who surrender a covered weapon or magazine through a buy-back program [S2].

Requires law enforcement to be notified when a prohibited person tries to buy a grandfathered semiautomatic assault weapon, and directs ATF to develop a framework for classifying firearms by how lethal they are and to build a database tracking mass shootings and the guns used [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers, who would lose the legal market for the rifles, pistols, shotguns, and magazines the bill covers; current owners face new storage duties, and private transfers of grandfathered guns require dealer background checks. Taxpayers fund the buy-back compensation and the new ATF tracking systems.

drawbacks.text: The grandfather clause keeps every existing covered weapon and large-capacity magazine in circulation, so the bill would not remove any gun already in private hands, only stop new sales and manufacturing [S2].

The definition of a covered weapon turns on features like a pistol grip, folding stock, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud rather than how fast the gun fires, and opponents of such bans argue that feature-based definitions sweep in firearms by cosmetic details while leaving similar firepower available in other designs [S3].

Opponents of restrictions on these firearms argue such bans do not stop determined criminals, who can obtain weapons through illegal markets, and that the restrictions burden law-abiding owners — a standing objection to every federal assault weapons bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill had passed, the main gain would be a shrinking supply of new military-style semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines over time, with current owners largely unaffected aside from storage and transfer rules. The costs fall on manufacturers and dealers in a defined market segment and on owners' convenience, and the grandfather clause means any public-safety benefit would arrive slowly. Honest supporters would acknowledge the feature-based definition is debatable and that a ban limited to future sales cannot address guns already in circulation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Frederica Wilson of Florida introduced the bill on June 28, 2018, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count was zero [S4].

On August 6, 2018, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, and no further action followed before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers lost nothing, since the ban never advanced; gun owners also avoided the new storage and transfer requirements.

for.name: Rep. Frederica Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing; it was sent to the crime subcommittee and died there.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority party of the 115th House
against.what_they_did: Never brought an assault weapons ban to the House floor during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only backer in Congress was its Democratic sponsor; it drew zero cosponsors, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill outlaws new manufacture, sale, and import of the semiautomatic rifles, pistols, shotguns, and over-10-round magazines it names, closing a product line worth a large share of industry sales. The grandfather clause protects owners of guns already sold, so the industry keeps the installed base but loses the future market [S2, S3].

Retailers would lose the legal market for covered weapons and large-capacity magazines, and would take on a new duty: running background checks before any private sale or transfer of a grandfathered assault weapon. The bill converts some of them into fee-earning background-check intermediaries, but the core effect is a smaller addressable market [S2].

Current owners keep their guns, but must store them securely where prohibited people could access them and use a licensed dealer for private transfers. Owners of the many hunting, sporting, and competition models listed in the exempt appendix are unaffected [S3].
